edits.fix: Use the standard footer with an id on every page, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / K1-1", in place of the bare page number.

edits.quote: Find as many ways as you can, using different blocks each time.
edits.fix: "Different blocks each time" can be read as never reusing a color. Say what counts as new, e.g. "Find as many different mixes of blocks as you can." There are 7 mixes (6g; 4g+1b; 2g+2b; 3b; 3g+1r; 1g+1b+1r; 2r) for the 9 boards.
Coloring needs crayons or colored pencils, and the materials list has only pencils. Add crayons to the adults' prep list, or have children trace the blocks as in P5.

edits.quote: Cover each shape with blue rhombuses ... Find all the different ways. (three one-unit hexagons and four 2-1-1 hexagons)
edits.fix: The unit hexagon's blue-only coverings were already found in P1, and the 2-1-1 hexagon has only 3 coverings, so this is over in a few minutes. Replace the three unit hexagons with a 2-2-1 hexagon (6 coverings) and give about 8 actual-size boards.

Say whether a turned copy counts as different. The unit hexagon's two coverings are turns of each other, so without a rule a child cannot tell when they are done. Add the rule the 4-5 pages use: a turned copy drawn differently counts as new.

edits.quote: Packet ends after P5 with a third of page 5 blank
edits.fix: A quick K-1 child finishes in about 30 minutes, which is the organizer's 'ends too early' complaint. Add one more substantial hands-on problem of about 15 minutes, e.g. build-your-own shapes on an actual-size triangle grid that blue rhombuses cannot cover, or bigger fewest-blocks boards.

k-1.summary: A clean, concrete K-1 set with correct actual-size boards and real entry points to both kernels: fewest blocks (answers 3, 3 and 6), yes/no boards that blue rhombuses cannot cover, and fewest-green triangles (2, 3, 4). P5 mostly repeats P1 and is too small, 'different' is undefined in P1 and P5, and a quick child runs out about ten minutes early.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>" on every page.

edits.quote: Can it be done?   yes   no (repeated under all four boards in P1 and again under J-M in P4)
edits.fix: The problem already says to decide whether it can be done. Under each board print only "yes   no".

edits.quote: Each board below is the same hexagon with two small triangles colored black.
edits.fix: The diagrams show this. Start with "Cover the white part of each board with blue rhombuses, or decide that it cannot be done."

edits.quote: Explain why every covering of board G uses at least 4 green triangles, no matter where you put the blue rhombuses.
edits.fix: This prints the answer to P2's board G. Rewrite as "Explain why no one can cover board G with fewer green triangles than your best covering." Then keep the side-10 question (answer 10).

edits.quote: Try to make a board that needs as many green triangles as possible when you cover it with blue rhombuses and green triangles. What is the most you can make it need?
edits.fix: This is a max-min question, and a child can read it as 'use lots of greens' (16). Say that even the best covering must use many greens, e.g. "Draw a board of 16 small triangles in one piece so that even its best covering needs many green triangles. How many can you force?" (The maximum is 6, e.g. a row of 11 with 5 up-triangles on top.)
An invention problem needs several attempts, and this grid holds one or two 16-triangle boards. Give P6 a full page of actual-size triangle grid.

grades-2-3.summary: The strongest band. All boards and expected answers check out: A and C are unbalanced boards with an even number of triangles and no covering; J and M are unbalanced; K and L can be covered; the fewest greens is n; chevrons cannot help; and the 16-triangle maximum is 6. Together they develop the up/down coloring argument from trying, through proof, to invention. The edits are small: repeated labels, one printed answer, an ambiguous max-min prompt in P6, and too little grid space.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>" on every page.

edits.quote: Find all the different ways to cover board A ... (board A with four small pictures)
edits.fix: Board A (2 coverings) is immediate for grades 4-5 and repeats K-1's P5. Drop A and its pictures, and keep B (3) and C (4) as the data for the top-edge-10 question (answer 11).

edits.quote: Board with a top edge 10 small edges long: _____ ways (top of page 2, split from its question on page 1)
edits.fix: Keep P1 on one page. Removing board A frees enough room to put the answer line and explanation space under board C.

edits.quote: Shade both chains in each covering of board D that you drew in Problem 2, and write their letters.
edits.fix: This is twelve rote shadings before the real question. Cut it, and let the worked example plus the four board-E letter pairs carry the problem (pairs 1 and 3 exist, pairs 2 and 4 cross at the first row).

Drawing all 20 coverings at 0.3-inch triangles takes about 20 minutes and stands between the children and P6-P7. Ask for the number and how they know it is complete, and leave the 25 boards as workspace.

edits.quote: Cover board E any way you like, and write the letters of its two chains. Make one move, as in Problem 3, and write the letters again. Try this with many different moves.
edits.fix: The step-by-step experiment protocol and 'try this with many different moves' should go. Ask directly: "What does one move do to the letters of the two chains?"

edits.quote: Explain why it takes at least 8 moves to get from S to T.
edits.fix: This prints the answer to P3's S-to-T question (8; S = RRLL/RRLL and T = LLRR/LLRR). Rewrite as "Explain why no one can get from S to T in fewer moves than your answer to Problem 3."

grades-4-5.summary: Mathematically rich and correct throughout. B, C and the top-edge-10 board give 3, 4 and 11 coverings; D has 6; E has 20; the move counts are S-T 8, S-U 3 and U-T 5; two of the chain pairs exist and two do not; and the parity argument is sound. The band builds kernel 2 from flips through ribbons to parity. It carries far more than 40 minutes, with heavy reading and some directed sub-steps (shading D's chains, the P6 protocol), and P7 prints P3's answer.

overall.strongest: Grades 2-3 develops the coloring obstruction through a well-chosen sequence of correct actual-size boards, from trying, through explaining impossibility, to inventing a worst board.
overall.weakest: K-1 ends about ten minutes early for a quick child, and its last problem largely repeats the first one's hexagon.
